analysis.one_liner: Provides free hepatitis C cures to Medicaid patients, prisoners, the uninsured, and Indian Health Service patients.
analysis.headline: The bill would spend about $9.8 billion to provide free, curative hepatitis C drugs to Medicaid and CHIP enrollees, prisoners, the uninsured, and Indian Health Service patients, but it has sat untouched in the Senate HELP committee since its June 4, 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a national program to eliminate hepatitis C, a curable virus that destroys the liver. It has the federal government buy hepatitis C drugs under a five-year subscription deal with manufacturers and give them free to low-income Medicaid and CHIP patients, people in prison, people without insurance, and patients of the Indian Health Service. It also funds testing and outreach grants, waives Medicare copays for these drugs from 2027 to 2031, and appropriates roughly $9.8 billion to pay for it.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the populations that carry the heaviest hepatitis C burden and the least ability to pay: Medicaid and CHIP enrollees, people in federal and participating state prisons and jails (including people who started treatment behind bars and need to finish it after release), people with no health insurance, and patients served by the Indian Health Service. Medicare beneficiaries would also stop paying copays and deductibles for hepatitis C antivirals from 2027 through 2031. States, community health centers, opioid treatment programs, Ryan White clinics, and correctional systems would receive grants to find, test, and treat people.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income, uninsured, and incarcerated hepatitis C patients

how_it_helps.text: People in the covered populations would be entitled to hepatitis C drugs with no cost-sharing at all — no copay, deductible, or coinsurance.
States that opt in must drop prior-authorization requirements for hepatitis C screening and treatment, removing the paperwork hurdle that insurers commonly use to delay these drugs.
People who begin treatment in a participating state or local prison or jail would get the rest of their cure and a referral to ongoing care upon release, instead of being cut off mid-treatment.
Medicare beneficiaries would pay no deductible, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing for hepatitis C antivirals for plan years 2027 through 2031.

Federal grants would fund outreach, screening, and treatment coordination through states, community health centers, opioid treatment programs, tribal health programs, Ryan White clinics, and correctional facilities.

The government would use competitive bidding to buy drugs under a five-year subscription model — paying a fixed annual amount for unlimited cures — the approach states like Louisiana used to slash the per-cure price.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill directly appropriates $5.5 billion plus $4.283 billion for fiscal year 2025 (available through fiscal 2031), and the Medicare cost-sharing waiver shifts those drug costs into the Medicare program, which taxpayers and premiums fund. The bill also exempts subscription-program prices from Medicaid's 'best price' rules, which reduces one form of downward pressure on government drug prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $9.783 billion for fiscal year 2025 out of the Treasury, a substantial new federal expenditure at a time of large deficits.

Prices charged under the subscription program are carved out of Medicaid's 'best price' and average manufacturer price calculations, shielding manufacturers from rebates those rules would otherwise trigger on other government purchases.
Providers, pharmacies, and dispensing sites are barred from using any other federal drug discount program, including the 340B program, for hepatitis C drugs obtained through the program.
Participation by state Medicaid and CHIP programs and state and local correctional systems is optional, so coverage would have gaps wherever states decline to join.
The free-drug entitlement is limited to citizens and a long list of specified legal immigration statuses, excluding undocumented people diagnosed with hepatitis C.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is large and unusually concrete: hepatitis C is curable with a short course of pills, and untreated infection leads to cirrhosis and liver cancer, so curing the disease in high-burden, low-income populations saves lives and avoids expensive downstream care. The subscription model uses competitive bidding, which historically cut per-cure prices dramatically in state deals. The honest costs are that $9.783 billion is real money, the bill hands manufacturers guaranteed revenue with a carve-out from Medicaid best-price rules, and the subscription structure pays a fixed amount annually whether or not projected numbers of patients actually get treated. On balance, a well-designed bill whose main weakness is the concessions it makes to the drug industry to get the purchase done.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on June 4, 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Cassidy, a Republican of Louisiana who chairs the HELP committee, and Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat of Maryland, introduced the bill on June 4, 2025.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
It has attracted one cosponsor and no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action has occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet: the bill is simply waiting. The status quo persists — drug manufacturers keep selling these cures at negotiated private prices, and the patients the bill would treat remain untreated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill awaits committee action

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-LA); lead sponsor and Chairman, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cure Hepatitis C Act of 2025; as HELP chairman, controls whether the committee ever marks it up.

for.name: Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by the bill's own sponsor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 4, 2025 and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan on its face — a Republican chairman sponsoring with a Democratic cosponsor — but there have been no votes, so no partisan split is on the record.

industries.industry: Brand-name hepatitis C drug makers (e.g., Gilead, AbbVie)
industries.note: The bill guarantees manufacturers a five-year, taxpayer-funded subscription customer and carves the negotiated prices out of Medicaid 'best price' rules, while barring 340B discounts on program drugs. Patients get a free cure, but the industry locks in a large new revenue stream on terms it helped design.
Pharmacies register with the program to dispense the free drugs and receive government-paid dispensing fees at customary regional rates.
The bill funds government purchase and distribution of point-of-care hepatitis C tests and up to $20 million to support development of new diagnostic tests, expanding the market for screening tools.

industries.industry: Community health centers, Ryan White clinics, and opioid treatment programs
industries.note: These safety-net providers would receive grants to expand testing, case management, and hepatitis C treatment for their patients.

Insurers must waive all cost-sharing for hepatitis C antivirals from 2027 through 2031, raising their drug costs; they can absorb this through bids and premiums, part of which the federal government pays.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress runs through January 3, 2027. With only two sponsors, no cosponsor momentum, and no committee action months after referral, the bill's most likely path is death in committee — a familiar fate for earlier versions of the Cure Hepatitis C Act. Its realistic hope is being folded into a larger must-pass health or spending package; its chairman-sponsor could schedule a markup at any time, but has not.
